questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A king's law set down in writing
questions.learningObjective: explain why a ruler had a code carved on a public monument
questions.stem: A king of a river-valley state has his judges' decisions collected, arranged by subject, and carved on a tall stone set up in a temple courtyard, where the text opens by praising the king for protecting the weak and ending the strong man's power. Which feature best explains the choice to carve it at all?

options.text: A public text lets the king advertise a rule he will enforce, which is a claim about his own rule and not only a record of decided cases
A carved text cannot be altered by a later king, so the decisions are permanently fixed
options.misconception: believes stone insulates a law from later revision

options.text: The judges stopped hearing disputes once the cases were written down, since writing settled them
options.misconception: supposes a written record ends the need for a court

options.text: The stone told litigants which side of a dispute the king had already decided, so no hearing was needed
options.misconception: turns a published rule into a list of prejudged verdicts

questions.explanation: Publishing a law is an act of sovereignty as much as an act of record-keeping, because a text that anyone may read and any judge may cite converts a decision into a rule, and the praise at the head of the stone is doing the same work on the king's character that the case list does on his competence. Nothing about stone prevents a later ruler from superseding a clause, and courts kept hearing cases for centuries after such collections existed, which is exactly why the display mattered: it was addressed to a reader rather than to a bench. The distractors each mistake an advertisement for a permanent rule, a record for a substitute for a hearing, or a code for a set of verdicts already handed down.
questions.hint: Ask who is being addressed by a text put where a crowd can read it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A king's law set down in writing
questions.learningObjective: identify what a retributive clause in a law code actually claims
questions.stem: One of the best-known clauses in that same carved text provides that if a man puts out the eye of another, his own eye is to be put out, and a few lines further on the text provides that a rich man who puts out the eye of a poor man is to pay a fine. What does that pair of provisions do?

options.text: It fixes the consequence by the injury done, except that the law grades the penalty by the rank of the wrongdoer
It shows the code abolishes differences of rank, since both penalties are fixed in advance
options.misconception: reads a rank-graded penalty as the abolition of rank

options.text: It makes the injured party choose the penalty, since the law offers two alternatives in every case
options.misconception: supposes the litigant a choice the text does not give

options.text: It applies the same penalty to a rich man and a poor man, since the injury is the same in both cases
options.misconception: ignores the rank clause it is being asked to read

questions.explanation: Read as one rule about consequence and one qualification about rank, the pair is coherent: the injury sets the norm, and the social position of the offender is allowed to shift what is paid rather than what is done. That combination is what the two clauses actually say, and it is also why later readers have found the same text usable as a claim about proportionality and unusable as a claim about equality, since a fine is a purchasable outcome. The distractors each eliminate one of the two things the provisions do, and one reads them as though neither existed.
questions.hint: Ask what the two provisions share, and what the second one changes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A king's law set down in writing
questions.learningObjective: weigh a legal collection against a statute book
questions.stem: A river-valley king has his judges' rulings gathered into one carved monument. Nearly two thousand years later, an emperor in the eastern Mediterranean commissions a lawyer to reduce the accumulated rulings of the Republic and the Empire to a single authoritative text and have it published. Which account best fits the pair?

options.text: The first settles what judges had decided and the second makes a disputed corpus usable by settling which version counts
The first created law from nothing and the second only tidied what the first produced
options.misconception: invents a direct line from one monument to the other

options.text: The second was needed because the first monument had been destroyed, leaving no rulings to collect
options.misconception: supposes a destruction the pair does not mention

options.text: Both did the same work, and the later one differs only in the medium used for the text
options.misconception: reduces a change of purpose to a change of technique

questions.explanation: The two projects answer different questions, which is why the later one is not a repetition. A carved collection of decisions states what a particular court concluded, and it says nothing about which of two competing opinions is right, so it can accumulate contradiction indefinitely. A compilation undertaken to make the material authoritative has to answer the conflict question, and does so by designating a text as the version that counts, which is a different operation from collecting rulings at all. The distractors each assert a causal line, a destruction, or an identity of purpose that the pair does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what a compilation of rulings cannot do that a declared edition of them can.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A king's law set down in writing
questions.learningObjective: state what a jurists' digest does and does not claim
questions.stem: A compiler's instruction to his team reads: go through the treatises and the recorded judgments of the jurists of our own time, and from what they have written select what is sound, discard what is merely clever, and arrange what remains under heads a practitioner can use; where opinions conflict, note the disagreement rather than resolve it. Read that instruction: what does it commit the compiler to?

options.text: A selection under arranged heads that leaves conflicts visible, so completeness is disclaimed in favour of usability
A complete transcript of every opinion, since the instruction names no stage at which anything is dropped
options.misconception: reads an instruction to discard as a promise to keep all

options.text: A new code of law made by the emperor's own judgment, since a compiler may settle what the jurists disputed
options.misconception: turns a compilation into original legislation

options.text: A study of what jurists argued, with the compiler's preference stated for each disputed question
options.misconception: supplies a verdict the instruction says to withhold

questions.explanation: The instruction is explicit about two things and silent about a third. It commands a selection, so the result is by design not a transcript, and it requires arrangement under practical heads, so the organising principle is usefulness to a litigant rather than chronology or authorship. What it refuses is adjudication, since it tells the team to record a disagreement rather than resolve it, and that refusal is what distinguishes a digest from a code of law. The distractors each claim a completeness, an authority, or a preference that the text specifically declines.
questions.hint: Ask what the instruction says to do when two authorities disagree.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A king's law set down in writing
questions.learningObjective: trace the condition under which a codified law survives
questions.stem: A river-valley code carved on stone is copied for some centuries, then the empire that read it falls apart; the eastern Mediterranean text of a millennium later, compiled by decree, is taught in universities and still used in courts to argue about obligations and ownership. Which comparison best explains the difference?

options.text: The later text survived because the institutions that taught and applied it were continuous, not because the words were better
The later text survived because it was longer, and length is what carried it through the fall of the older code's readership
options.misconception: credits bulk of text rather than continuity of use

options.text: The older code failed because stone was a poor medium, whereas paper and parchment outlast carved monuments
options.misconception: invents a medium explanation for a difference in readership

options.text: The two survived or failed for opposite reasons, so no single account can cover both cases
options.misconception: declares the comparison unanswerable rather than weighing it

questions.explanation: A legal text is carried by whoever has to apply it next, which is an institutional fact rather than a property of the words, and the two cases differ precisely there. A collection tied to a legal order that dissolved lost its audience with the courts, officials and litigants that made it worth copying, whereas a compilation that became part of how a trained legal profession was formed acquired a constituency that survived every political change around it. That is why a text can be in continuous use for a very long time without being especially well written, and why an admirable code can disappear without anybody deciding to suppress it. The distractors each substitute a textual property, a technical one, or a refusal to compare.
questions.hint: Ask who had a reason to keep copying each text after the century in which it was made.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship extended by decree
questions.learningObjective: identify who a grant of citizenship leaves out and why that matters
questions.stem: An imperial decree of the early third century states that the burden of citizenship shall no longer fall on any person who has lived all his life in an alien's city, that all who have previously held citizenship shall retain it, and that nothing in this is to extend to those who have come into the empire's power by surrender, nor to the freed. Read that decree: what does its drafting establish?

options.text: A very wide grant that is still bounded, so the decree's usefulness lies in which categories it names and which it refuses
An unconditional grant, since the closing sentences only explain the decree and add no restriction
options.misconception: reads the exclusions as commentary rather than as limits

options.text: A grant confined to the leading towns, since living long in a city is the only route the decree names
options.misconception: converts a route into an exclusive requirement

options.text: A declaration about the future, since the decree deals with a city population that did not yet exist
options.misconception: assumes a retrospective decree rather than a prospective one

questions.explanation: The decree is drafted in the register of an exception to a rule, and that is the whole reason its categories are so specific. The burden falls on anyone long resident in a subject city, which sweeps in the overwhelming majority of the subject population, and existing citizens are protected, which closes the obvious loophole. The two categories left out are named because the author thought about them: those who came by surrender are treated as defeated rather than resident, and the freed are treated as dependent rather than as members of a city. The distractors each deny one half of what the text does, which is to be generous in scope and explicit in limit.
questions.hint: Ask why a decree that enfranchises most people still needs two named categories.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship extended by decree
questions.learningObjective: weigh the competing explanations offered for a mass grant of citizenship
questions.stem: Historians still argue about why the early-third-century decree enfranchised nearly the whole free population. One argues it completed a two-century development and gave legal form to a society that had already become Roman. Another argues the emperor needed the number of taxable and litigant subjects, and that the decree's timing tracks the cost of a war. Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.text: The two readings predict different things about the decree's timing, so the timing is the place to test them rather than the motives of the emperor
The first reading is correct because a legal development of that length cannot be an accident of fiscal need
options.misconception: settles a live dispute by asserting one side's authority

options.text: The decree settles the matter, since a law states its own reasons and needs no external evidence
options.misconception: treats a decree as a self-explaining document

options.text: The dispute is unresolvable because the emperor's motives are by nature unavailable to historians
options.misconception: concludes from the nature of the subject rather than the evidence

questions.explanation: Competing explanations earn their keep by predicting something other than themselves, and here the two readings come apart on a checkable point: a developmental account expects the grant to appear late in a long sequence, while a fiscal account expects it to cluster around the moment of greatest fiscal strain. Neither reading can be dismissed on the strength of its own elegance, because both fit the fact that the grant came, and the honest position is that the evidence available constrains them unevenly rather than eliminating either. The distractors each avoid the comparison by appealing to authority, to the document's own voice, or to an assertion about what historians can never know.
questions.hint: Ask what each explanation would have to predict about when the decree appeared.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship extended by decree
questions.learningObjective: explain how a change in legal status redistributes an obligation
questions.stem: Before the decree, the burdens of the imperial tax system fell on a small body of citizens whose members were recruited locally, and the subject population generally held local rights only. After the decree, the subject population is enrolled in a single legal category alongside the old citizen communities. Which consequence follows from the change in status?

options.text: The population that had previously been outside the citizen tax rolls is now inside them, so the same assessment reaches many more people
The local rights that the subject population held are abolished, since one category cannot contain two sets of rights
options.misconception: assumes a unified category destroys rights held underneath

options.text: The old citizen communities lose their standing, since a single category admits only one kind of member
options.misconception: turns inclusion of others into dispossession of the original

options.text: Litigation becomes impossible, because two legal systems cannot be applied within one empire
options.misconception: supposes a single category disables the courts entirely

questions.explanation: A status is a bundle of obligations as much as a bundle of rights, and the decree moves a very large population from a category in which the imperial tax system largely did not reach them into one in which it does, which is the mechanical difference that a fiscal explanation finds congenial. What the change does not do is strip the rights that the subject population already held locally, since those arose from local membership and were never the content of the grant. That is also why the aftermath is not simply a victory for anyone: a wider legal category spreads the imperial system across more people and costs some of them obligations they had not carried. The distractors each convert a widening of coverage into an abolition, a dispossession, or a paralysis.
questions.hint: Ask what a legal category does to the people moved into it that it did not do to those already in it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Citizenship extended by decree
questions.learningObjective: connect a measure of enfranchisement to a number of citizens
questions.stem: A study of the citizenship of the empire puts the number of citizens at roughly four to seven in every hundred of the subject population at the death of the first emperor, and treats the figure as a range rather than a point. What is the most defensible reading of that range?

options.text: The record cannot support a single figure, so the range marks the width of the evidence rather than a disagreement about what happened
The truth is somewhere in the middle, so the arithmetic mean of the two ends is the best available estimate
options.misconception: treats an evidence range as two measurements of one thing

options.text: The lower end describes the cities and the upper end the countryside, so the two numbers are about different populations
options.misconception: invents a geographic split the study does not claim

options.text: The range indicates the study's confidence interval, so anything outside it is known to be false
options.misconception: reads a documented range as a statistical interval

questions.explanation: A range in this position is doing the work of an honest statement about how much the record supports, and the studies that publish it are careful to say so: the ancient sources give totals of different scope, the census returns that survive are partial, and no register survives that would settle the figure. Taking a midpoint would manufacture a precision the evidence does not contain and would also imply that the two ends measure the same quantity, which they may not. The defensible move is to say what the range is a range of, and then to ask what the conclusion actually needs: whether the pre-decree citizen body was a small minority is not in doubt at either end. The distractors each convert a statement about evidence into a statistical result, a geographical claim, or a verdict on other work.
questions.hint: Ask what a range is a range of when the underlying sources disagree in scope.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price list issued by edict
questions.learningObjective: identify the step a price edict leaves out
questions.stem: In the early fourth century an emperor, who has just remade the coinage, issues a list setting the maximum price and wage for more than a thousand goods and services across the empire, threatens death for anyone charging more, and orders the list posted in every province. Within a few years the list is largely disregarded and is later withdrawn. Which step does the design lack?

options.text: It fixes the price without attaching an inspector to the moment of exchange, so compliance depends on a buyer choosing to complain
It fixes no prices at all, since a list of maxima leaves every seller free to set any figure
options.misconception: misreads a ceiling as an absence of a price

options.text: It fixes the price but not the wage, so sellers and workers never agree on what a fair price is
options.misconception: ignores the wage schedules the edict also contained

options.text: It fixes the price for the provinces only, since a posting order cannot reach the capital
options.misconception: supposes a territorial limit the posting order contradicts

questions.explanation: A ceiling is only as strong as the moment at which somebody acts, and a price posted in a provincial town creates no such moment: a seller who quietly charges more is discovered only if a buyer complains, a buyer who quietly pays more never complains, and a complaint requires a buyer who knows the ceiling and has a reason to invoke it. That is the missing link, and it explains both why the edict could be disregarded within a few years and why the emperor's own currency reform, which changed what a coin was worth rather than what a price should be, met a different reception. The distractors each deny a part of what the text contains or invent a limit it has no basis for.
questions.hint: Ask who acts at the moment a price is charged above the stated figure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price list issued by edict
questions.learningObjective: read an enforcement clause against the likely level of compliance
questions.stem: A preserved copy of the price edict's closing provisions runs: a trader who, in a place where the maximum is known and there is no war, buys where the price is low and sells elsewhere at the maximum is to be put to death; and anyone who knows of such a practice and does not report it is to suffer the same penalty. Read that clause: what does it tell you about how the edict expected compliance to be achieved?

options.text: It expects enforcement to come from mutual informing, so private persons are made agents of the rule rather than the state's officers
It expects the number of transactions to be small enough for the authorities to witness them all
options.misconception: supposes a scale of trade that makes witnessing possible

options.text: It expects sellers to record their prices openly so that buyers can check them
options.misconception: converts an informing duty into a publication requirement

options.text: It expects the penalty to be applied only where a buyer has already lost money by paying too much
options.misconception: narrows the trigger to a private loss the clause does not mention

questions.explanation: The clause reveals that the authorities expected the rule to be enforced by the people inside the trade rather than by officers standing beside every sale, because it makes silence itself a punishable offence. That is a coherent response to a rule covering more than a thousand items across an empire, and it is also a fragile one: a duty to inform is only as strong as the informer and the belief that somebody is listening, and both weaken as the rule's currency falls. The fact that the harshest available penalty was legislated and compliance nonetheless faded is itself evidence about the mechanism. The distractors each substitute a different enforcement technology, none of which the text describes.
questions.hint: Ask who the edict enlists in the work of detecting a breach.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price list issued by edict
questions.learningObjective: place a price edict inside a currency reform
questions.stem: The same emperor, in the months around the price edict, issues separate currency decrees that redesign the coinage, raise the face value of the silver coin, and decentralise the mints. Historians differ over whether the price list was a response to the coinage change or to a longer inflation. Which statement about the relationship is soundest?

options.text: The two measures are two attempts on one problem, so the timing is close enough that neither can be read as a response to the other with confidence
The price edict must be a response to the coinage decrees, since the decrees are dated first in the series
options.misconception: infers a causal order from a sequence of dates alone

options.text: The price edict must be independent of the coinage decrees, since a list of prices does not mention coins at all
options.misconception: treats silence about a subject as independence from it

options.text: The coinage decrees are the only plausible reading, and every economist who examined them reached that conclusion
options.misconception: converts one scholarly view into unanimity

questions.explanation: Two measures issued within months of each other by the same man against the same symptom are properly understood as one policy in two parts, because a currency change moves the level of prices and a price list tries to hold a level against that movement, and an emperor who wanted stable accounts would reach for both. What the closeness of the dates cannot settle is direction of causation: a text may answer a change or reveal that the change was needed, and the edicts are silent on each other. The honest reading is therefore about the policy as a whole rather than about a trigger, and it leaves room for the longer inflation argument without dismissing it. The distractors each manufacture a causal order from dating, from silence, or from an appeal to unanimity that does not exist.
questions.hint: Ask what two measures issued together by one man against one problem can and cannot tell you about direction.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A price list issued by edict
questions.learningObjective: explain why a repealed edict does not prove it had no effect
questions.stem: Explain why the fact that a price edict was withdrawn within a few years, and that the wider troubles it addressed were not settled in that emperor's reign, is weaker evidence against the measure than it first appears, and say what evidence would settle the question.

answer.exemplar: Withdrawal is a statement about the emperor's judgement at one moment, not a measurement of what the edict did, and an edict that fixed a visible number for more than a thousand items across an empire has effects that outlive its enforcement whatever the enforcement was. A ceiling that the state has announced can still move a seller's expectation, a buyer's complaint, a creditor's valuation of a debt, or a magistrate's sentence, and none of those channels requires anyone to prosecute a breach, so the edict can have lowered the general level at which prices were discussed even while the market cleared above it. Meanwhile the troubles it addressed were not confined to prices, and a later authority re-issuing a different monetary measure is equally consistent with an edict having helped and with its having been useless. The evidence that would actually settle the question is therefore distributional and chronological: price series from named towns showing whether the level moved at the edict and how soon it moved back, court records showing how often the maxima were invoked, and inscriptions or letters showing that people knew the figures. Any of those would turn the argument from a sequence of events into a measured one, and the absence of a clear result in the emperor's own lifetime is not the same as a clear result against the measure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An industry taken into state hands
questions.learningObjective: identify what a state monopoly on a basic commodity is for
questions.stem: A Han government, in the second century before the common era, takes the production and sale of salt and the mining of iron into its own hands, appoints officials to run both, and forbids private dealing. The stated reason is that the revenue is needed to meet costs the treasury cannot otherwise meet. Which feature does the arrangement exploit?

options.text: Salt and iron are consumed by everybody, so a state that controls their supply can draw on the entire population rather than on taxable landholders
Salt and iron are the two goods whose price never moves, so controlling them guarantees the revenue
options.misconception: assumes a fixed price for the two commodities

options.text: Salt and iron are heavy, so a state that makes them pays less to move them than a merchant would
options.misconception: locates the advantage in transport rather than consumption

options.text: Salt and iron are the goods the population buys most often, so the state earns on every single purchase
options.misconception: confuses frequency of purchase with a basis for taxation

questions.explanation: A monopoly is a way of choosing a base, and the reason these two were chosen is that they are not taxes on land and are not avoidable: a household cannot salt its food or leave its tools unmade, so the demand for them is spread across the whole population, including the very people who hold no taxable land and appear on no register of households as liable. That makes the arrangement attractive precisely in a period of prolonged war, when the cost of maintaining a large army is enormous and the alternative is a tax on those best able to bear it. The distractors each attach the measure to a property of the commodities that is not the one doing the work, and one of them simply repeats the sense of the arrangement without explaining it.
questions.hint: Ask what is common to every household about the two goods the state took over.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An industry taken into state hands
questions.learningObjective: state the two positions argued in a recorded debate about a monopoly
questions.stem: A generation after the monopolies were imposed, a written debate is staged at which officials answer critics and are themselves answered. Which of the following are positions actually represented in that debate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ending the monopolies would empty the treasury and leave the state's soldiers unfunded, so the revenue has to come from somewhere
The monopolies enrich the state at the expense of the people who must buy salt and use iron, and should be ended
Iron smelting on a large scale requires capital and fuel that private households cannot assemble, which is an argument for the state's scale
The debate settled the question, and the monopolies were abolished within five years of the discussion
options.misconception: invents an outcome the recorded debate did not produce

questions.explanation: The three substantive positions are all present because the recorded exchange is structured as an answer and a counter-answer rather than as a single verdict, and each of the three does real work. The fiscal argument is that the revenue funds an army and therefore buys protection, the interest argument is that the cost falls on consumers who cannot avoid the purchase, and the scale argument concedes the interest case partially by pointing out that the production itself required capital beyond a household's reach. The fourth is not a position in the debate at all but a claim about its outcome, and the state of the monopolies after the exchange shows no such resolution. What the debate demonstrates is that a fiscal necessity and a hardship can both be true at once, which is why the document is more useful as evidence of the disagreement than as evidence of a verdict.
questions.hint: Ask which three claims are arguments in the exchange and which is a claim about what happened afterwards.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An industry taken into state hands
questions.learningObjective: weigh a state monopoly against what a recorded debate reveals
questions.stem: The written debate staged between officials and critics of the salt and iron monopolies survives complete enough to show both sides, and the monopolies continue afterwards. Which account of the relationship between the text and the policy is soundest?

options.text: The text shows the policy was contested on stated grounds, and the policy's continuation shows the contest did not remove it, which are two separate findings
The text shows the critics won, since a government that keeps a measure is a government that accepted the objections
options.misconception: reads a continuation of policy as a defeat for its critics

options.text: The policy's continuation shows the text must have been falsified, since an honest record would show a change
options.misconception: treats an unchanged outcome as proof of a doctored text

options.text: The text shows the officials had no case, since a policy needing such a defence was a policy without support
options.misconception: judges a policy by the need it had to be defended

questions.explanation: The survival of the exchange and the survival of the policy are two pieces of evidence about two different things, and keeping them apart is what makes the document usable. A recorded debate with real arguments on both sides establishes that the measure was contested in terms its contemporaries understood, which is a fact about the politics and about the range of views a literate official class could hold. The measure's continuation establishes that the contest did not reverse it, which is a fact about the balance of forces rather than about the truth of either case. Neither finding cancels the other, and reading either as a verdict on the other is the standard way a rich document gets over-read. The distractors each convert a continuation into a defeat, a defeat into a forgery, and a defence into an admission of guilt.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two facts is evidence about, before asking what they imply together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An industry taken into state hands
questions.learningObjective: compare a monopoly that funds an army with one that restricts a trade
questions.stem: One government takes the salt supply into its own hands and sells it to the public at a fixed figure; another gives one merchant an exclusive right to bring a particular commodity into the country and forbids all others to do so. Which statement about the two best captures the difference in what each can be used for?

options.text: The first can fund ordinary spending because its revenue is collected from many, while the second can change who is in a particular trade, which is a distribution of rights
The first is a tax and the second is a regulation, so the two cannot be compared at all
options.misconception: declares the arrangements incomparable without trying

options.text: The first is a monopoly and the second is a tariff, so the second can raise the same revenue at lower cost
options.misconception: relabels the two and invents a revenue equivalence

questions.learningObjective: state what a positional recording system can and cannot do
questions.stem: An Andean state keeps its accounts on cords hung from a primary cord, where each pendant is divided into sections by the position of its knots, the highest power of ten nearest the primary cord and the units at the far end, and the numbers are read outward. Suppose a pendant carries a long knot with seven turns at its end, preceded by three single knots and then four. What does that pendant record?

The number seven hundred and thirty-four, since the longest knot governs the leading place
options.misconception: reverses the reading direction, starting from the free end

options.text: The number four hundred and seventy-three, since the middle group stands for the tens rather than the hundreds
options.misconception: misassigns the middle group to the wrong decimal place

options.text: The number seven thousand three hundred and four, since a long knot always marks a multiple of a thousand

A long knot is a compact way of recording a value in the units place, and the system also permits a different number to follow it on the same cord, which is a saving a writer would use. questions.explanation: The loss is severe but it is a specific kind of loss, and specifying it tells the historian what is recoverable. What is gone is the archive that would have spoken in the administration's own categories, so the reconstruction has to begin with somebody else's description, and every such description is a translation in the double sense of a rendering into another language and a rendering into the categories of the describer's own state. That is why a reading based on outsiders' accounts can be so much weaker than the archive-based account of a rival period, and why an important question in this field is what the empire's own terms were. What the loss does not do is establish that the system was absent, that its content was harsh, or that nothing can be known, since the descriptions of outsiders survive in numbers and can be compared with one another. The distractors each convert a missing archive into a verdict on the system or on the historian's task.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of evidence is left once an empire's own records are gone.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A succession crisis at the top
questions.learningObjective: identify what a disputed succession does to a conquered empire
questions.stem: The ruler of a large Andean empire dies, apparently of a disease introduced by newcomers, and the succession is unsettled: his presumptive heir also dies, and two of his sons, one holding the imperial capital in the south and one holding the northern seat with the army, begin a civil war. Which feature of that situation best explains the empire's later defeat?

options.text: The two halves of the empire spent the next several years fighting each other, so the force that had been built for expansion was committed to a civil war when outside pressure arrived
The empire had no law of succession at all, so any death of a ruler was followed by a general collapse
options.misconception: supposes an absence of rules that the contested case contradicts

options.text: The disease made the population too weak to resist, since a mortality of that kind always produces a military collapse
options.misconception: reduces a military outcome to epidemiology

options.text: The northern seat was too far from the capital for the empire to be governed, so the centre had already lost the north
options.misconception: treats a distance from the capital as a cause of defeat

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a diversion of the state's own instruments, and it needs no assumption about a law of succession to work: a war between a claimant in the south holding the capital and a claimant in the north holding the army consumes the manpower, the treasury and the administrative attention that the empire had built, and it does so for years rather than months. A state that is fighting within its own borders cannot present the same force abroad, and an army that is being paid and fed by a treasury whose revenue is being spent on a civil war is a different army from the one that conquered. The disease matters here as a trigger and not as a cause, since it removed a ruler and an heir in quick succession, which is what made the dispute possible at all. The distractors each propose a structural defect, a demographic explanation, or a geographical one that the sequence does not require.
questions.hint: Ask what the state's fighting force was doing in the years before the outside attack.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A succession crisis at the top
questions.learningObjective: weigh the competing claims made about a ruler's death
questions.stem: A widely repeated account holds that a ruler of the Andean empire died of the smallpox brought by newcomers, and that his successor did so too, which is why the empire was delivered into the hands of invaders. Other accounts note that the newcomers had themselves lost a large part of their force to the same disease at the point of first contact, and that the ruler's own successor was in the north. Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.text: The first account identifies a real mechanism, a disease arriving with the newcomers, and the second identifies a real check on its weight, since the same disease reached the newcomers, so neither settles the timing of the ruler's death
The second account refutes the first, since a disease that reached the invaders cannot have caused a death in the capital
options.misconception: refutes a causal claim by showing the cause was also active elsewhere

options.text: The first account is the better one, because the second introduces a fact about the outsiders that the record does not support
options.misconception: dismisses a second datum without evaluating it

options.text: The two accounts are about different rulers, so the disagreement is an artefact of the comparison
options.misconception: resolves the tension by supposing a mistaken identity

questions.explanation: Both halves of this are true and they pull in different directions, which is why the useful item is the mechanism plus the check. A disease arriving with an invading force is well documented as a catastrophe for the populations it meets, and the arrival of such a disease is a real and sufficient explanation for the deaths at the top of a ruling house, and therefore for the succession crisis that followed. But the same disease reached the invading force, which is why the invaders did not simply take the empire, and that fact is a check on any account that makes the disease the whole story of the conquest. Neither the identity of the disease nor the timing of the ruler's death follows from the argument, and both are contested in the sources. The strongest formulation is the one that names the mechanism, names the limit, and declines to date a death that the record does not date. The distractors each treat the two halves as competitors rather than as complement and constraint.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two claims adds that the other does not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A succession crisis at the top
questions.learningObjective: assess the agency of a subject population in a conquest
questions.stem: An outside force of a few thousand men overruns a large empire whose ruling house is weakened by a civil war, and much of what follows depends on the fact that peoples inside the empire who had long resented the empire's rule formed alliances with the newcomers and supplied guides, interpreters and troops. Which account of the conquest follows from that?

options.text: The empire's defeat required the cooperation of some of the peoples it governed, so its fall is evidence about the empire's internal divisions and not only about the newcomers
The empire's defeat was purely a matter of numbers, since a few thousand men cannot take an empire without allied help
options.misconception: makes allied cooperation a consequence of a numerical shortfall

options.text: The peoples who allied with the newcomers had always preferred them, so the empire was never supported by its own population
options.misconception: generalises from some allied groups to a preference for outsiders

options.text: The conquest shows the empire lacked the resources to resist, so its population cannot have been numerous
options.misconception: infers a population size from a military outcome

questions.explanation: The scale of the force on one side against the size of the state on the other is the reason the alliances have to be part of the explanation, since a few thousand men cannot occupy a large state over a long period without local cooperation in supplies, guides, translation and administration. Once the alliances are in the account, the conquest stops being a story about the invaders' strength and becomes evidence about the empire, since a state that some of its own subject peoples were willing to help an outsider defeat is a state whose rule was not accepted throughout, and the grievances that produced that willingness were a condition of the outcome. The distinction matters for what follows, since a conquest that requires local allies calls for an account of what those allies wanted, and a conqueror who depends on them is constrained by them. The distractors each reduce the outcome to a single dimension, whether numbers, preference, or size.
questions.hint: Ask what a conquering force of that size must obtain from inside the state it takes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A succession crisis at the top
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a succession dispute becomes a conquest
questions.stem: The four developments below occur in a recognisable order in the collapse of a large Andean empire. Place them.

options.text: A disease brought by newcomers reaches the population, and the ruling house loses a ruler and an heir in quick succession
Two claimants, one based in the imperial capital in the south and one in the northern seat with the army, contest the succession
The civil war between the claimants runs for years and the empire's forces and revenues are committed to it
Outside forces, allied with peoples inside the empire who had opposed its rule, move in against a state whose army is elsewhere

questions.explanation: The four steps form a chain in which each is the condition of the next, and the order is not a matter of preference. A disease can only remove a ruler and an heir if it has reached the population, so the epidemic precedes the succession crisis, and a succession crisis needs the two claimants to exist, which requires the earlier deaths. The contest then has to run before the empire's forces are elsewhere, since a state that has just resolved a disputed succession has not spent years consuming its own army, and it is precisely that expenditure that makes the state's forces unavailable when the last step arrives. The last step depends on the third, because an outside force can only move in against a distracted state if the state's attention and forces are committed inward. The distractors would each require an outcome before the condition that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask what has to have happened for each of these to be possible at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An alliance against a neighbour
questions.learningObjective: identify what a subject people gains from allying with an invader
questions.stem: For years a large inland power has taken tribute from towns and villages outside its own territory, including military service from their inhabitants, and a number of those towns have petitioned repeatedly against it. A neighbouring group of newcomers arrives and offers alliance, and some of the towns supply troops and guides. Which statement about that alliance is soundest?

options.text: The towns are acting on a grievance the power had already been told about, so their cooperation is a response to a specific prior experience rather than a preference for outsiders
The towns have always preferred newcomers, since a power that took tribute was never their own ruler
options.misconception: generalises from a period of extraction to a lasting preference

options.text: The towns ally because they expect the newcomers to tax them more heavily, since a foreign army is a more reliable tax collector than a nearby one
options.misconception: supposes a heavier tax as a reason to welcome extraction

options.text: The towns have no agency in the matter, since a decision taken by a few leaders binds a whole population in a conquest
options.misconception: removes the possibility of a collective decision by a subject population

questions.explanation: The petitions are the fact that carries the argument, because they put the extracting power on notice and establish that the towns' dissatisfaction was articulated before the newcomers arrived, which is a very different situation from a population discovering a preference for foreigners. A town that has petitioned and not been relieved has a grievance that is specific, dated and addressed, and an offer of alliance is evaluated against that record. The towns are also not simply passive in this: they supply troops, guides and intelligence, which means somebody in each town has weighed the offer and concluded that the alternative was worse, and the terms they obtain are evidence of what they thought they were worth. That is not the same as saying they chose what happened next, since an ally that wins will impose its own terms. The distractors each turn a dated grievance into a standing preference, invert the direction of the interest, and remove collective agency.
questions.hint: Ask what the towns had already said to the power before the newcomers appeared.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An alliance against a neighbour
questions.learningObjective: weigh the terms of an alliance between an invader and a subject people
questions.stem: A treaty made between a neighbouring group of newcomers and a subject town records that the town shall keep its own god and its own ruler, shall govern itself by its own custom, and shall not be asked for tribute; and it records that the newcomers shall be given the use of the town's market and shall receive the townspeople as allies. Read that text: what does it establish about the balance between the two parties?

options.text: The townspeople had something specific to protect and the newcomers had something specific to want, so the agreement is a trade between two positions rather than a surrender
The town had been fully independent before the treaty, since a party cannot surrender what it never possessed
options.misconception: assumes the treaty's recitals describe the prior state

options.text: The newcomers were the weaker party, since a treaty naming their own obligations must have been imposed on them
options.misconception: reads a list of obligations as evidence of weakness

options.text: The town's own custom is guaranteed in perpetuity, so no later demand could lawfully touch it
options.misconception: takes a promise in a treaty as an unbreakable guarantee

questions.explanation: Both sides' clauses are specific and both sides' clauses are the things the other side wanted, which is the signature of a negotiated instrument rather than a capitulation. The town is guaranteeing the outsider's religion and political form and giving the outsider access to its market, which it would not do if the newcomer were the party in need, and the newcomer is guaranteeing the town's autonomy and promising not to demand tribute, which it would not promise if it were already the master. The balance is therefore legible from the text, and it is the most important thing a treaty of conquest tells us, because it records what each side believed it could not get by other means. None of that guarantees durability, since a promise of autonomy is exactly the kind of thing a conqueror revises when it can, and the clause about the town's god is the one a conqueror is most likely to keep and the one a successor is most likely to test. The distractors each misread the recitals, invert the balance, or convert a promise into a guarantee.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two sides' clauses would that side have found costly to concede.

questions.topic: An alliance against a neighbour
questions.learningObjective: explain how an alliance changes the terms of a conquest
questions.stem: A large empire is destroyed by a small invading force, but the destruction depends on alliances made with peoples the empire had ruled, and the terms afterwards vary from one region to another, with some communities keeping a ruler and a custom and others being ruled directly. Which account best fits that variation?

options.text: The variation reflects the terms each ally managed to extract, and it is therefore a measure of the empire's internal divisions as much as of the invader's policy
The variation reflects the invader's own preference, applied differently according to how much each region had to be conquered
options.misconception: reduces a negotiated outcome to a policy of the victor

options.text: The variation reflects each region's own prior status, so a community that had been ruled before the empire was treated as it had been treated then
options.misconception: assumes a single consistent prior status explains the variation

options.text: The variation is evidence that the allies were fighting among themselves, since a united cause produces uniform terms
options.misconception: infers internal disagreement among allies from a difference of outcome

questions.explanation: A region that kept a ruler and a custom made a bargain and got terms, and a region ruled directly is one that was taken without an ally, so the variation is a map of which parts of the empire had someone willing to deal with the newcomers. Reading the pattern that way tells the conqueror's history from the inside, since it measures how far the old state's authority had failed, region by region, rather than how far the new one had reached. It also tells us something about the allies, because a community that obtained terms was a community that had organised enough to negotiate, and the terms themselves are the best evidence of what it thought it could enforce. The invader's policy is visible in the pattern too, but it is the pattern's floor rather than its whole explanation. The distractors each reduce the variation to one party's preferences or to a single prior status, and one infers allied disagreement from a difference in outcomes that is fully explained without it.
questions.hint: Ask what a community had to have done differently to end up with a ruler of its own.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shock to the labour ratio
questions.learningObjective: trace what a wage cap fixed below the market produces
questions.stem: After a mortality of the order of a third to two fifths, a legislature fixes the maximum daily wage of a master mason at three pence and of a labourer at a penny and a half, the levels recorded before the mortality. One of the largest employers in the country, an abbey, is paying six pence a day in the same year. Which reading of those figures is best supported?

options.text: The cap sat at half what one employer paid, so the rule and the practice were not describing the same labour market
The cap sat at twice the practice, so the employer was underpaying by half the lawful rate
options.misconception: inverts the ratio of the cap to the payment

options.text: The two figures describe different crafts, so no comparison between them is possible
options.misconception: supplies a craft distinction the figures do not mention

options.text: The employer's figure proves the cap was never published, since a published cap would have been obeyed
options.misconception: infers non-publication from a single departure

questions.explanation: The two figures are of the same trade, in the same country, in the same year, and the larger is exactly twice the cap, which is the sort of coincidence that lets a reader check a rule against practice inside a single institution. A cap fixed at the pre-mortality level is a cap fixed below the market that a shortage of workers has created, so the gap between the cap and what one large employer paid is not a curiosity but a measurement of the gap the rule was trying to close. From there the rest follows: a rule that binds employers and not workers is enforced unevenly, because a worker who refuses the capped rate can leave and find someone else, while an employer who offers more is the party visibly breaking the law. The figures therefore support a conclusion about the mechanism and about enforcement, and they do not by themselves support a conclusion about whether the shortage was real. The distractors each invert the ratio, invent a distinction, and infer a failure of publication from one practice.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two figures is bigger, and what a cap below the market rate is.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shock to the labour ratio
questions.learningObjective: weigh competing accounts of the effect of a mortality shock on wages
questions.stem: A mortality that killed perhaps a third or more of a population is followed by grain prices that rise steeply and stay high, and by wage rates that manorial accounts record as rising over the following century. One account says wages roughly doubled and labourers were unusually well off for a century. Another says the price rise cancelled the wage rise, so real purchasing power did not improve, and adds that the accounts that show doubling come from institutions with an interest in reporting high wages. Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.text: The two accounts are about different quantities, one money wages and one purchasing power, and the second's point about who kept the accounts is a reason to ask which series is used rather than to discard the series
The first account is right, since a doubling of the money wage cannot be cancelled by a rise in the price of grain
options.misconception: assumes a wage rise must show up in purchasing power

options.text: The second account is right, since an institution's interest invalidates every wage figure it recorded
options.misconception: discards a body of evidence on the ground of the recorder's interest

options.text: The dispute cannot be settled, because the grain price series and the wage series were kept by different people
options.misconception: concludes from separate provenance that no comparison is possible

questions.explanation: Money wage and real wage are different quantities and a mortality shock moves them in different directions, since the shortage of workers bids up what a worker can be paid while the shortage of labour to work the land cuts the harvest and bids up grain, so the two series must be compared rather than either read alone. The second account's contribution is to make the comparison explicit, and its further point about the provenance of the wage figures is a methodological warning rather than a refutation: a series kept by employers and estates is a series with a reason to record what was paid, which is a reason to compare several series from different kinds of institution and to look at how far apart they lie. That procedure is available and has been carried out, which is why the question is better described as one of interpretation than of mere inaccessibility. The distractors each treat a real series as decisive, discard evidence on the ground of interest, and mistake separate provenance for incommensurability.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two accounts are describing the same quantity.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shock to the labour ratio
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a mortality shock reaches a labour market
questions.stem: The four developments below occur in a recognisable order after a mortality of a third or more of a population. Place them.

options.text: Wage rates in money begin to rise, as employers compete for a much smaller number of workers
The legislature fixes wages and food prices at levels recorded before the mortality, and limits the movement of workers
Grain prices rise steeply and remain high, as fewer hands work the land and more mouths compete for what is harvested
Employers begin offering more than the capped rate in practice, and the rule is enforced unevenly

questions.explanation: The four belong to one sequence and the dependency is economic before it is administrative. A smaller population means fewer workers, so the price of labour rises, and it means more competition for the harvest, so the price of grain rises; both of those are the market adjusting to the shock, and neither is a consequence of any statute. Only once the market has moved does the legislature have something to respond to, which is why the fixing of wages and food prices follows the two price rises rather than preceding them, and why the levels chosen are the pre-shock ones, since a government legislating in a crisis reaches for the last figure it can remember as normal. The last step follows from the mismatch: if the cap is below what the market pays, then the only way for an employer to get a worker is to offer more, and the rule's bite depends on which party is the visible lawbreaker. The distractors would each require a statute to have caused a price it was legislating against.
questions.hint: Ask which of the first two events a legislature is responding to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Holding ships without closing the port
questions.learningObjective: explain why a port city used isolation rather than closure
questions.stem: A small Adriatic trading city, whose soil will not feed its people and which buys grain by ship from Sicily and the Levant, keeps an island and a headland outside its walls where arrivals from places with plague must wait out a fixed number of days before entering, with a scribe, guards and a person to dig graves assigned to them, and it records the rule in its own law book. Read that arrangement: what is it?

options.text: A measure that accepts the cost of a delay to protect a trade it cannot give up, and the staffing detail shows it was administered rather than merely declared
A measure that shows the city had closed its port, since arrivals were held outside the walls for so long
options.misconception: conflates a hold on arrivals with a closure of the port

options.text: A measure taken after the disease had passed, since the city had no need to hold arrivals before an outbreak
options.misconception: supplies a date for the measure the text does not give

options.text: A measure of religious observance, since the fixed number of days comes from a scriptural figure
options.misconception: substitves a motive the text does not state for the one it does

questions.explanation: The arrangement is legible as a choice between two costs, and the account supplies both of them. A city whose food comes by sea cannot close its port without starving, so it takes the other cost and holds arrivals, which delays trade and is expensive in a way its own council can calculate. The detail that most repays attention is the staffing, since a scribe, guards, cleaners and a grave digger are the components of an administrative apparatus rather than a sentence in a statute, and their presence tells a historian that the rule was operating and at what running cost. Recording it in the law book then fixes it as a standing obligation rather than a temporary measure, which matters because the city remained exposed to outbreaks for three decades. The distractors each convert an arrival hold into a closure, supply a date, or supply a motive the text does not mention.
questions.hint: Ask what the city would have to give up if it closed the port, and what the staffing detail shows.

questions.topic: Holding ships without closing the port
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a port practice became a general rule
questions.stem: The practice of holding arrivals below developed in stages, and the four developments below occur in that order. Place them.

The period is lengthened to forty days, and the word for the hold is coined from the number
Neighbouring maritime powers copy the practice, and a certificate of health begins to travel with the ship
A purpose-built place of isolation is built outside the walls, replacing the open ground and the islands

questions.explanation: The sequence runs from an improvised local rule to a formalised international one, and each step presupposes the one before it. There is nothing to lengthen until there is a period, and the naming follows the period rather than the other way round, since a number that has become the name of the practice is evidence that the practice has settled into a routine. The certificate can only travel once several ports are using the same rule, because a document asserting that a place is healthy is worth nothing if the place it names does not apply the same standard, which is what makes this a step of a shared practice rather than of one city's law. The purpose-built building comes last in this sequence because it is a refinement, and the accounting matters: the improvised version, with its islands and its wooden huts, is what ran for over a century and a half before the buildings went up. questions.hint: Ask what has to exist before a number can be lengthened, named, or certified elsewhere.
